“Dog lovers” vs dog lovers when it comes to greeting dogs! ETA: “dog lovers” could also be replaced with “uniformed, uneducated, and/or inconsiderate dog lovers” vs “informed, educated, and considerate dog lovers” if that makes you more comfortable 🫶 One of my biggest pet peeves is people baby talking to my dog and pretending like I’m interrupting? Bizarre! And in case you didn’t know because it’s something that’s been so normalized, putting your hands in dogs’ faces is unsafe. Dogs don’t need to sniff you up close like that and it’s putting unneeded pressure on them (often leading to bites). The best way to greet a dog is calm, neutral, and honestly just ignoring them. If you want to say hi to a dog, ask the owner first. Try to make yourself small by turning to the side and crouching. Allow the dog to approach you first. Some dogs are super friendly and love people! This doesn’t mean it’s ok to pet or approach without asking their handler! The safest way to greet any dog is by admiring from afar. Admittedly, if I know someone’s dog well, I might be a bit of the former “dog lover” and be excitedly greeting them 😂 It’s different when you know the dog! “But she’s just a corgi…”  Meet Maple the 4 year old Corgi.  Sweet in the right moments… but dangerous in the wrong ones. Resource guarding food and household items. Multiple bites on owners and family members. Reactive to other dogs on walks, barking & lunging. And now there’s a baby in the home. During the evaluation, Maple tried to bite me multiple times. Not because she’s a “bad dog”… But because she’s been making decisions for a long time without clear direction. No real structure. No consistent boundaries. No clear communication or expectations. And when you let “dogs be dogs” they do just that.  This is the part people struggle with.. You can love your dog deeply and still be missing the leadership they actually need. Honest question… Do you think dogs like Maple know they’re doing something wrong… or are they just doing what’s always worked for them? #DogTraining #dogtrainer #dogsoftiktok #dogs #dog

Most owners don’t realise you can spot heart and respiratory disease at home before your dog looks unwell. It takes about thirty seconds, costs nothing, and it’s something vets ask owners to do all the time. It’s called the resting respiratory rate. When a dog’s heart starts to struggle, fluid builds up in the lungs and they breathe faster while resting. That tends to happen before any coughing or tiredness shows up. How to do it: 	•	Wait until your dog is asleep or fully settled. Not panting, not just back from a walk, not lying somewhere warm. 	•	One breath is the chest rising and falling once. 	•	Count the breaths for 30 seconds and double it, or count a full minute if your dog will stay put. 	•	Skip it if they’re dreaming and twitching, as that throws the number right off. A healthy dog at rest usually breathes fewer than 30 times a minute, and most sit around 15 to 25. The single reading matters less than the pattern, so jot it down a few times a week until you know what’s normal for your dog. Ring your vet if that resting rate settles consistently above 30, or creeps up over a few days. Take it seriously if your dog already has a heart murmur. It won’t replace a proper check-up, but for at-risk dogs it’s one of the most useful things you can keep an eye on.  #DogHealth #HeartDisease #VetTips #DogCare #PetHealth
